This removes every recorded clip and its notes from the phone. Copies you have already shared are not affected.

A clip stores up to 60 seconds of raw microphone audio on this phone, in the app\'s private storage, together with the time it was made, what the app decided, and the notes you enter. It records everyone within earshot, so let the people singing know. Nothing is uploaded; a clip only leaves the phone when you choose Share. You can delete all clips at any time.
The A your band tunes to. Sharp and flat are counted from it. Keys are found the same way whatever it is set to.
Numbers shows chords by their place in the key (Nashville numbers): 1, 4, 5, 6m.

Basic Pitch is a small neural network that hears each note being played. In our tests on recorded guitar and on synthesized instruments it named chords and keys right a little more often, and held up better when the music was out of tune. It shows chords about a second later. Try both. Its cost shows under Details.

CREPE is a small neural network trained on singing. On 40 recorded singers it found the right note more often, most of all with background noise. It is new here: try both with your singers. Its cost per frame shows under Details.
Do Re Mi uses fixed Do: C is always Do.
Each song is saved here when you press New song or Stop, once KeyCatch has found its key. The list stays on this phone.
This removes every saved song from the list. Lists you have already shared are not affected.

We built KeyCatch to listen the way a musician does: it hears the notes and chords and makes its best guess at the key. Most of the time that guess is right. Sometimes it isn\'t, and here\'s when to keep an ear out.
It can get it wrong when…
If people are singing between notes, KeyCatch has to guess. You\'ll see “best guess” under the key when that\'s happening.
Groups often creep sharp or flat through a long song. KeyCatch follows them, but it can fall behind or settle on the key next door.
A lift for the last chorus takes a few seconds to catch. When a new song starts, press New song so the old one doesn\'t get in the way.
Major or minor isn\'t clear yet.
C major and A minor use the same notes. KeyCatch waits for clues, like where the lines come to rest, so give it a moment.
Talking, clapping, a loud fan or a phone in a pocket can drown out the music. Hold the phone closer to the sound.
The song doesn\'t stay in one key.
Blues, modal tunes and songs full of passing chords can pull it toward a neighbouring key.
In Band and Guitar modes the tempo can lock onto double or half the real speed. Tap the BPM number to switch between them.
Singing rarely gives a steady beat, so in Voices mode you tap the tempo in yourself.
Chords show up about a second late, because KeyCatch listens a little ahead to be sure.
Rich chords are shown as the nearest simple one. A Cmaj9 might show as Cmaj7 or C.
If your band tunes to something other than A = 440, set it in Settings so “in tune” means what you expect.
KeyCatch is new, and we haven\'t tried it in every kind of room or with every kind of band yet.
Think of KeyCatch as a second pair of ears, not the final word. When it matters, trust your own ears too. If something looks off, New song gives it a fresh start.

KeyCatch can hear notes with two open research models: CREPE, by Jong Wook Kim, Justin Salamon, Peter Li and Juan Pablo Bello (MIT licence), and Basic Pitch, by Spotify\'s Audio Intelligence Lab (Apache 2.0). Text is set in Manrope (SIL Open Font Licence) and the icons are Google\'s Material Symbols (Apache 2.0). Their licences ship with the app.
Everything happens on your phone. No audio leaves it unless you choose to share a recorded clip yourself.
